# 1. Introduction

The Nobel Prize is one of the most well-known awards in the world. It recognizes people for their achievements in science, literature, peace, and other fields.

For this assignment, I will use the Nobel Prize API to explore gender representation among Nobel laureates. My goal is to understand the differences between male and female laureates and see how female representation has changed over time.

I will focus on four research questions:

1\. How many Nobel laureates are male and female?\
2. How has the number of female Nobel laureates changed over time?\
3. Which Nobel Prize category has the highest percentage of female laureates?\
4. Which countries have produced the most female Nobel laureates based on birth country?

# 2. Planned Approach

I will use R to collect and analyze JSON data from the Nobel Prize API. First, I will use the jsonlite package to retrieve the data and load it into R. I will also use the tidyverse package to clean, filter, and organize the data. Next, I will analyze the data to answer my four research questions.

For the first question, I will count the number of male and female laureates and calculate their percentages. For the second question, I will use the award years to examine how the number of female laureates has changed over time. For the third question, I will calculate and compare the percentage of female laureates across Nobel Prize categories. For the fourth question, I will use birth country information to identify the countries with the highest number of female laureates. I will use the current birth country names provided by the Nobel Prize API. Finally, I will create bar charts and a line chart using ggplot2 to present my results.

# 3. Anticipated Challenges

One possible challenge will be extracting information from the JSON data. Some fields, such as birth country and Nobel Prize category, are stored inside other fields. Another challenge may be missing values. Some records may not include gender or birth country information. I will need to check these records and handle missing values before the analysis. Some laureates may have received more than one Nobel Prize. I will need to be careful not to count the same person more than once in each analysis.

# 4. Code Base

## 4.1 Required Packages

I will use the jsonlite package to read JSON data from the Nobel Prize API. I will also use tidyverse to clean, organize, and analyze the data.

```{r}
library(jsonlite)
library(tidyverse)
```

## 4.2 Retrieve JSON Data

I will use the Nobel Prize API to collect information about Nobel laureates. I will also check how many records are included in the data.

```{r}
url <- "https://api.nobelprize.org/2.1/laureates?limit=1028"

nobel_data <- fromJSON(url, flatten = TRUE)

names(nobel_data)
```

## 4.3 Explore the Dataset

I will convert the laureates data into a data frame and check the number of rows, columns, and variable names.

```{r}
laureates <- as_tibble(nobel_data$laureates)

dim(laureates)

names(laureates)
```

The dataset contains 1,028 rows and 110 columns. It includes information about Nobel laureates, such as gender, birth country, and Nobel Prize details. I will use these variables to answer my four research questions.

## 4.4 Select Relevant Columns

I will select the columns needed for my analysis. I will use the laureate ID, gender, birth country, and Nobel Prize information.

```{r}
nobel_clean <- laureates %>%
  select(
    id,
    gender,
    birth_country = `birth.place.countryNow.en`,
    nobelPrizes
  )

glimpse(nobel_clean)
```

The dataset contains 1,028 rows and 4 columns after selecting the relevant variables. These columns include laureate ID, gender, birth country, and Nobel Prize information. Some birth country values are missing. The Nobel Prize information is stored as a list.

## 4.5 Check Missing Values

I will check for missing values in the selected columns. This will help me understand which information is missing before starting the analysis.

```{r}
colSums(is.na(nobel_clean))
```

The dataset has 28 missing values in the gender column and 31 missing values in the birth country column. There are no missing values in the ID and Nobel Prize columns. I will exclude missing values when they are needed for each analysis.

## 4.6 Prepare Nobel Prize Data

I will organize the Nobel Prize information into a separate data frame. This will help me analyze the award years and categories.

```{r}
nobel_awards <- nobel_clean %>%
  select(id, gender, nobelPrizes) %>%
  unnest(nobelPrizes)

glimpse(nobel_awards)
```

The new data frame contains 1,036 rows and 23 columns. It includes information about award years, Nobel Prize categories, and laureate gender. The number of rows increased from 1,028 to 1,036 because some laureates received more than one Nobel Prize.

## 4.7 Q1: How Many Nobel Laureates Are Male and Female?

I will count the number of male and female Nobel laureates and calculate their percentages. I will exclude records with missing gender information and count each laureate only once.

```{r}
gender_summary <- nobel_clean %>%
  filter(gender %in% c("male", "female")) %>%
  distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  count(gender) %>%
  mutate(percentage = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 2))

gender_summary
```

The results show that 931 Nobel laureates (93.1%) are male, while 69 laureates (6.9%) are female. This shows a large gender difference among Nobel laureates.

### 4.7.1 Gender Distribution of Nobel Laureates

I will create a bar chart to compare the number of male and female Nobel laureates.

```{r}
ggplot(gender_summary, aes(x = gender, y = n, fill = gender)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(percentage, "%")),
    vjust = -0.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Gender Distribution of Nobel Laureates",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Number of Laureates"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The bar chart shows that 93.1% of Nobel laureates are male, while only 6.9% are female. This shows a large gender gap in Nobel Prize history.

## 4.8 Q2: How Has the Number of Female Nobel Laureates Changed Over Time?

I will examine how the number of female Nobel laureates has changed over the decades. I will group the award years into decades and count the number of female laureates in each decade.

```{r}
female_by_decade <- nobel_awards %>%
  filter(gender == "female") %>%
  mutate(
    awardYear = as.integer(awardYear),
    decade = (awardYear %/% 10) * 10
  ) %>%
  distinct(id, decade, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  count(decade, name = "female_count") %>%
  complete(
    decade = seq(1900, 2020, 10),
    fill = list(female_count = 0)
  ) %>%
  arrange(decade)

female_by_decade
```

The number of female Nobel laureates has generally increased over time. In the 1950s, no women received a Nobel Prize. The number increased to 11 in the 2000s, 13 in the 2010s, and 16 in the 2020s. This shows an upward trend in recent decades. However, the 2020s are not yet complete.

### 4.8.1 Female Nobel Laureates Over Time

I will create a line chart to show how the number of female Nobel laureates has changed over the decades.

```{r}
ggplot(female_by_decade, aes(x = decade, y = female_count)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1900, 2020, 10)) +
  labs(
    title = "Female Nobel Laureates Over Time",
    x = "Decade",
    y = "Number of Female Laureates"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The line chart shows that the number of female Nobel laureates has generally increased over time, especially after the 1990s. In the 1950s, no women received a Nobel Prize. The number increased from 7 in the 1990s to 16 in the 2020s. The 2020s have the highest count so far, but this decade is not yet complete.

## 4.9 Q3: Which Nobel Prize Category Has the Highest Percentage of Female Laureates?

I will compare the percentage of female laureates across Nobel Prize categories. I will count male and female laureates in each category and calculate the percentage of women. I will count each laureate only once per category.

```{r}
female_by_category <- nobel_awards %>%
  filter(gender %in% c("male", "female")) %>%
  distinct(id, `category.en`, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(category = `category.en`) %>%
  summarise(
    total = n(),
    female_count = sum(gender == "female"),
    female_percentage = round(female_count / total * 100, 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(female_percentage))

female_by_category %>%
  mutate(female_percentage = sprintf("%.2f", female_percentage))
```

The Peace category has the highest percentage of female laureates at 18.6%, followed by Literature at 15.4%. Physics has the lowest percentage at 2.17%. These results show that female representation varies across Nobel Prize categories.

### 4.9.1 Percentage of Female Laureates by Category

I will create a bar chart to compare the percentage of female laureates across Nobel Prize categories. I will also display the percentages above the bars.

```{r}
ggplot(female_by_category,
       aes(x = reorder(category, -female_percentage),
           y = female_percentage,
           fill = category)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.2f%%", female_percentage)),
    vjust = -0.5
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title = "Percentage of Female Nobel Laureates by Category",
    x = "Nobel Prize Category",
    y = "Female Laureates (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

The bar chart shows that Peace has the highest percentage of female laureates (18.58%), followed by Literature (15.45%). Physics has the lowest percentage (2.17%), followed by Economic Sciences (2.97%). This shows that female representation is different across Nobel Prize categories.

## 4.10 Q4: Which Countries Have Produced the Most Female Nobel Laureates Based on Birth Country?

I will use birth country information to find which countries have the highest number of female Nobel laureates. I will use current country names and count each laureate only once.

```{r}
female_by_country <- nobel_clean %>%
  filter(gender == "female", !is.na(birth_country)) %>%
  distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  count(birth_country, name = "female_count") %>%
  arrange(desc(female_count))

head(female_by_country, 10)
```

The results show that the USA has the highest number of female Nobel laureates, with 18 women. France is second with 6, followed by Poland with 4. Canada and Iran each have 3 female laureates. These results show that the number of female Nobel laureates varies across birth countries.

### 4.10.1 Top 10 Birth Countries of Female Nobel Laureates

I will create a bar chart to compare the top 10 birth countries of female Nobel laureates. I will also show the number of laureates above each bar.

```{r}
ggplot(head(female_by_country, 10),
       aes(x = reorder(birth_country, -female_count),
           y = female_count,
           fill = birth_country)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = female_count), vjust = -0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Birth Countries of Female Nobel Laureates",
    x = "Birth Country",
    y = "Number of Female Laureates"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

The bar chart shows that the USA has the highest number of female Nobel laureates, with 18 women. France is second with 6, followed by Poland with 4. Canada and Iran each have 3 female laureates. The other countries in the top 10 each have 2. This shows a large difference between the USA and the other countries.

# 5. Conclusion

In this assignment, I used the Nobel Prize API to analyze gender representation among Nobel laureates. I collected JSON data and used R to clean, organize, and analyze the information.

The results show that most Nobel laureates are male (93.1%), while only 6.9% are female. However, the number of female laureates has increased over time, especially after the 1990s.

Peace has the highest percentage of female laureates (18.58%), while Physics has the lowest (2.17%). The USA has the highest number of female laureates based on birth country, followed by France and Poland.

Overall, this analysis helped me understand gender differences in Nobel Prize history. It also helped me practice working with JSON data, cleaning data, and creating visualizations in R.
